_readme: Hand-curated state data. Update once a year as states publish. Rate rule: if rate_published is set, it is shown as published; otherwise the page computes unfilled / (unfilled + filled) or unfilled / total from the components given here. 'basis' overrides the basis label. 'sy' is the school year a figure describes (used for plotting); 'agency_label' records the agency's own year label when it differs. 'measure' documents what each state counts; 'tier' is the comparability group shown on the page. Never enter an estimate: leave a value out and explain why in 'note'.

states.name: Illinois
states.definition: ISBE's Unfilled Positions collection, in FTE, by category. ISBE defines an unfilled position as one 'not filled by an appropriately-licensed, permanent educator as of Oct. 1.' That includes empty positions and positions covered temporarily by substitutes or contracted staff, even when the district is not actively recruiting (for example, a substitute expected to be hired once licensed). What makes a substitute-covered position unfilled is that it has no contracted, permanent holder, not the substitute's qualifications: a position covered by a fully licensed substitute is still unfilled, while a substitute covering for a contracted teacher on leave leaves the position filled. Interim administrators and licensed retirees hired back count as filled. ISBE's wording may also cover permanent staff without the appropriate license, but ISBE does not report how often that occurs; any such cases are bounded by the low overall rate. So these are ISBE-defined unfilled rates, not necessarily shares of empty positions. Not a full census: 92% of education entities (1,029 of 1,120) responded for SY25. ISBE's vacancy rate pairs each year's unfilled FTE with the prior year's filled FTE (filled counts are only final after the year ends): SY25 = SY25 unfilled / (SY24 filled + SY25 unfilled). SY23-SY25 rates are computed here from ISBE's published components and match ISBE's rounded figures. SY22 pairs SY22 unfilled with SY22's own filled count, a same-year pairing, so it is not strictly comparable to later years. SY26 is a rate published by ISBE. SY18-SY21 have unfilled counts only, with no denominator, so no rate exists. In the same report's superintendent survey, the number of teaching positions filled by substitutes or retirees rose from 276 (2019) to 1,159 (2025).

states.name: Virginia
states.definition: VDOE's Positions and Exits Collection. VDOE defines the rate as fall unfilled FTE teacher positions divided by total available FTE teacher positions. 2023-24 through 2025-26 are VDOE's published rates. 2022-23 is a third-party calculation (SwailLandis, March 2023) from VDOE's Staffing and Vacancy 'Build-a-Table' data; its denominator column is labeled 'FTE Teachers', so whether it includes the unfilled positions is unclear, and the same brief also cites a 2.6% figure. No exact 2021-22 rate exists in any primary source checked; only approximations (JLARC: 'about 2,600' vacant), so 2021-22 is left unplotted. VDOE also publishes a separate Summer and First Week of School Vacancy Report (since 2024), which counts a position as vacant if it is unfilled or filled with an unlicensed teacher and divides by the previous fall's teacher FTE. That report pools vacancies with unlicensed hires, so it is not used here; the rates shown are VDOE's fall figures, which its December 2025 release describes as based on positions and exits data.

points.note: No point: only approximations exist (JLARC 'about 2,600' vacant). An approximation is not a data point.

states.name: Michigan
states.agency: Michigan Department of Education and CEPI, analyzed by EPIC at Michigan State University (statutory Michigan Teacher Shortage Study)
states.timing: Fall snapshot of district personnel records (Registry of Educational Personnel)
states.definition: The Michigan Teacher Shortage Study, required by state law and prepared by EPIC at Michigan State University from state personnel records, counts a teaching position as vacant if it is 'either unfilled or temporarily assigned to a substitute, temporary employee, or outside contractor,' including positions posted but not yet filled and positions held for an employee on leave or on loan. Positions held permanently by under-credentialed teachers count as filled. The rate is FTE-weighted: vacant teaching FTE as a share of all teaching FTE. Districts were not required to report all vacancies until 2023-24, so earlier years are not shown, and the study's authors caution that the change between 2023-24 and 2024-25 may partly reflect better reporting. The 2023-24 rate appears only in a chart, so it is not plotted.

points.note: Published in the Michigan Teacher Shortage Study (January 2026): 'the overall vacancy rate of 2.8%' for fall 2024 (rounded to 3% in the report's headline). About 6% in urban districts, under 2% elsewhere.

measure.counted: Funded teaching positions unfilled or temporarily staffed in the fall
measure.includes_substitute_covered: Yes, and also positions held for staff on leave or on loan
measure.coverage: All districts (state personnel records); reporting required from 2023-24
measure.substitutes_short: Yes; also positions held for staff on leave

states.verification: Verified directly on 2026-10-10 against the January 2026 Michigan Teacher Shortage Study (definition of 'vacant' in the methods section; 2.8% in the vacancy section).

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.timing: October 1 snapshot (October 2 in 2023), Professional Staff Vacancy collection
states.definition: PDE's Professional Staff Vacancy collection (PIMS) defines a vacancy as 'an unoccupied position that has been board approved and posted to allow the LEA to proceed through the hiring process.' Positions staffed by long-term or day-to-day substitutes until permanently filled count as vacant (PDE flags them separately), as do positions with no designated staff. Positions held by someone on a Type 01 Emergency Permit count as filled. Rates are computed here, not published by PDE: classroom teacher vacancies (full- and part-time positions) divided by classroom teachers in PDE's Professional Staff Summary on the same snapshot date (full- and part-time headcount) plus the vacancies. Vacancies are positions and teachers are people, so the two units differ slightly. A few LEAs did not report (6 of 778 in 2025-26). From 2024-25 PDE collects vacancies quarterly; the October quarter is used here to match 2023-24.

points.note: 2,112 full-time and 44 part-time classroom teacher vacancies as of Oct. 2, 2023; 126,069 classroom teachers (Professional Staff Summary, Oct. 2, 2023). Rate computed here.

1,632 full-time and 27 part-time classroom teacher vacancies as of Oct. 1, 2025 (Q1); 128,699 classroom teachers (Oct. 1, 2025). Rate computed here.

states.name: Maryland
states.timing: First day of school (Annual Vacancy Data Collection); teacher counts as of October 15
states.definition: MSDE's Annual Vacancy Data Collection counts teacher vacancies on the first day of school, reported by local school systems in full-time equivalents. MSDE does not publish an operational definition and does not say whether positions covered by long-term substitutes count as vacant. Conditionally licensed teachers are reported separately (6,067 in 2025-26) and are not counted as vacancies, so the measure is not credential-based. MSDE publishes no rate. Rates are computed here: first-day vacancies divided by teachers in MSDE's Professional Staff by Assignment, Race/Ethnicity and Gender report for the same school year (all teachers, including those reported at central offices, as of October 15) plus the vacancies. Vacancies are full-time equivalents and teachers are a headcount, each counted once in their primary assignment, so the units differ slightly; the two counts are about six to eight weeks apart within the same school year. MSDE's March 2026 minutes note that falling vacancy counts may partly reflect positions cut locally, which state data do not capture. The 2023-24 count was 1,935.4 in MSDE's May 2024 presentation and 1,941.4 in later presentations; the later figure is used. The 2026-27 count (572) comes from the governor's release of Oct. 19, 2026, which rounds it and gives no date; it has no rate until MSDE publishes its October 2026 teacher count.

states.name: Iowa
states.coverage: Full-time teaching positions; includes positions filled by temporary or substitute staff
states.timing: Postings over the prior 12 months, collected each fall
states.definition: Districts are required by law to report full-time teaching positions 'that were advertised but not filled or that were filled with temporary/substitute staff.' The count is a 12-month flow: Iowa's spreadsheet for its latest release says it covers positions posted between August 20, 2024 and August 20, 2025. The rate divides by full-time teachers employed the previous fall, not by filled plus vacant positions. Iowa's press releases label each figure by the year it was collected and released; this page plots each figure at the school year its postings cover, one year earlier than the press-release label, matching the labels on Iowa's own September 2026 dashboard. A 1.12% figure for the latest year that circulated in news coverage does not match the agency's release (1.15%).

points.note: Published by Iowa DOE under the label 2022-23: 941 full-time positions, 2.63%. Presumed to cover postings from Aug 2021 to Aug 2022; the window is documented only for the latest year, and Iowa's own dashboard also labels figures by the earlier school year.

Published by Iowa DOE under the label 2023-24: 763 full-time positions, 2.03%. Presumed to cover postings from Aug 2022 to Aug 2023; the window is documented only for the latest year, and Iowa's own dashboard also labels figures by the earlier school year.

Published by Iowa DOE under the label 2024-25: 661 full-time positions, 1.75%. Presumed to cover postings from Aug 2023 to Aug 2024; the window is documented only for the latest year, and Iowa's own dashboard also labels figures by the earlier school year.

Published by Iowa DOE: 434 full-time positions, 1.15% of the 37,637 full-time teachers employed in fall 2024. Covers postings from Aug 20, 2024 to Aug 20, 2025 (per Iowa's district spreadsheet). Iowa's January 2026 press release labels this figure 2025-26; its September 2026 dashboard labels it 2024-25. 184 are special education.

Iowa DOE Teacher Pipeline Dashboard announcement, Sept 28, 2026

measure.denominator: Full-time teachers employed the previous fall (not filled plus vacant)

states.definition: CERRA's annual Educator Supply and Demand Survey of district personnel directors. Table 5 publishes vacancies and 'positions (authorized FTEs, excluding vacancies)' for each year, so the rate is computed here as vacancies / (positions + vacancies). Both counts include service positions as well as teachers (about 5,200 of the 56,500 positions in 2025-26 are service roles). Coverage varies by year: 71 to 83 reporting entities, and 2021-22 also includes career and technical centers and two state agencies.

states.name: Colorado
states.timing: Whole school year: 'unfilled' means unfilled for the entire year
states.definition: CDE's Educator Shortage Survey of districts and BOCES. CDE counts positions that 'remained unfilled throughout the school year', as a share of all teaching positions (from CDE's Human Resources snapshot). That is a much stricter test than an October 1 stock, which is why Colorado's rates are low. Positions filled through a 'shortage mechanism' (long-term substitutes, retirees, alternative or emergency licenses) count as filled: in 2025-26 that was 27.8% of open teaching positions. No 2024-25 rate exists: CDE's 2024-25 workbook has unfilled teaching FTE (254.64, summed from teaching endorsement areas) but no total-positions field.

nebraska.coverage: Teaching and specialist positions (including school counselors, psychologists, speech-language pathologists), public and nonpublic schools combined
nebraska.definition: NDE separates 'Vacant' (not filled at all) from the broader 'Unfilled' (left vacant, or filled by someone other than a fully qualified teacher). The summary totals combine public districts and ESUs with nonpublic systems, and include specialist roles such as school counselors, psychologists, and speech-language pathologists. Response was 97.7% for public districts but 57.8% for nonpublic systems (81.8% overall) in 2025-26. No total-positions denominator is published, so Nebraska contributes counts, never a rate.

snapshot.label: Start-of-year snapshots of vacant or unfilled positions
snapshot.text: These states report positions vacant or unfilled near the start of the school year, sometimes including positions covered temporarily by substitutes. They are the closest to one another and to the national School Pulse Panel, but differences in coverage, denominators, and definitions still limit comparisons across states.

different.label: Different measures: compare trends, not levels
different.text: Iowa counts a year's worth of postings that went unfilled or were covered by substitutes, divided by employed teachers. Colorado counts only positions that stayed empty all year. Each state's trend is informative, but their levels should not be set beside the others.
